The search found several third-party tools that sync MCP server configs from one canonical file to Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Gemini CLI. None of the results are official vendor features.

- **Claude Code as the source:** One project, sync-agents-settings, treats Claude Code as the master. It writes to Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, and several other tools, and it also syncs instruction files. It covers Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Kiro CLI, Cursor, and several others. Its config paths include ~/.gemini/settings.json for Gemini CLI and ~/.codex/config.toml for global Codex CLI config.
- **Claude config as input:** mcp-sync (ejfn) reads a Claude-format config as its source. It can also remove servers from targets that are missing in the source, using a `--prune` flag. Codex CLI config lives in ~/.codex/config.toml under an mcp_servers key, and Codex only supports stdio servers in that tool.
- **Dedicated canonical file:** Several tools use their own file. The Rust crate mcp-sync reads a single mcp.yaml and writes to Claude Code, Codex, and other targets. The EnjoyableWork mcp-sync uses ~/.config/mcp-sync/config.json as its single source of truth.
- **Multi-agent manager:** mcpport can list, lint, sync, and convert configs across Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, and Cursor. It uses a JSON target with comments, which Gemini CLI allows, and that target is read but never written, to avoid dropping the comments.

**Format gotchas:** The formats differ between tools. Codex uses TOML, and the HTTP field name varies. One guide notes that the protocol is portable but the config is not. Gemini CLI uses httpUrl for streamable HTTP, while Claude and Codex use url. Tools that sync secrets or scope need care with env-var handling.

Taken together, the results show a common pattern: pick one canonical file, then have a tool render it into each CLI's native format. I didn't verify whether any of these projects is actively maintained, and I didn't check whether Claude Code, Codex CLI, or Gemini CLI now offer native sharing of MCP config.

The search turned up documentation for Intellectronica's Ruler, a tool that manages one set of rules and MCP server settings across several coding agents, including Codex, Gemini CLI, and Claude.

- **Scope:** Ruler is an app that applies the same rules to all coding agents, and it's distributed on npm as @intellectronica/ruler.
- **Applying to specific agents:** Running `ruler apply` covers every configured agent, and the `--agents` flag limits a run to a subset, such as Claude alone (ruler apply --agents copilot,claude is the documented example).
- **MCP config targets:** The per-agent output files are listed in a table: Claude Code uses `.mcp.json`, OpenAI Codex CLI uses `.codex/config.toml`, and Gemini CLI uses `.gemini/settings.json` (the table maps each agent to its instruction file and MCP config path).
- **Where MCP servers are defined:** In v0.3.0, MCP servers are now configured in ruler.toml, with a legacy `.ruler/mcp.json` path still supported for migration.
- **Skipping MCP:** The `--no-mcp` flag skips MCP propagation during apply, per the same README excerpt that shows the apply examples.

Caveat: one search result is a fork (DVisionPRO/ruler) with the same project name, so I relied on the Intellectronica-linked sources for the details above. I didn't find release notes covering the newest version, so the file paths may have changed since the sources were written.

content.content:
**Install:** Build from source with `cargo install --path .`. The page doesn't mention a crates.io install.

**Commands:**
- `sync` (default): one-time sync to all targets. Options include `--scope global`, `--dry-run`, and `--clean`.
- `watch`: re-syncs when mcp.yaml changes.
- `init`: interactive wizard to create mcp.yaml.
- `validate`: checks mcp.yaml syntax and schema.
- `diff`: shows differences between the canon and current target configs.
- `completions`: generates shell completions for bash, zsh, and fish.

**Source file format:** A single `mcp.yaml` with a `version`, optional `plugins`, and a `servers` map. Local stdio servers specify `command`, `args`, `env`, `cwd`, and `enabled`. Remote servers set `kind: http`, plus `url` and `headers`. The canon can also be loaded from a URL.

**Targets:**
- Claude Code (CLI), Codex (OpenAI CLI), Antigravity (VS Code extension), and OpenCode are built in, along with custom targets loaded as dynamic libraries.
- **Gemini CLI is not mentioned on the page.**

**Global vs. project scope:**
- `--scope` accepts `global`, `project`, or `both` (default `both`).
- Global configs are user-level files. For example, Claude uses `~/.claude.json`, and Codex uses `~/.codex/config.toml`.
- Project configs live in the project root, such as `.mcp.json` for Claude and `.codex/config.toml` for Codex. The root is auto-detected from the git root unless you pass `--project-root`.

**Preserves other settings:** The page doesn't say whether unrelated settings in target files are preserved.

**Backups:** Before changing any file, mcp-sync creates a timestamped backup next to it, such as `config.json.bak.20260105-230041`.

**Dry-run:** `--dry-run` prints the changes without writing any files. Pairing it with `--verbose` shows more detail.

**License:** MIT.

content.content:
**mcp-sync** is a CLI that keeps local MCP server definitions in sync across AI clients.

- **Install:** Homebrew (`brew install EnjoyableWork/tap/mcp-sync`), Windows Package Manager (`winget install EnjoyableWork.mcp-sync`), Cargo (`cargo install enjoyable-mcp-sync`), or GitHub Releases archives.
- **Commands:** `init` imports existing definitions, `add` creates a server, `list` shows names without values, `test` runs a bounded STDIO check, `sync` applies changes, and `restore` reverts a file.
- **Source of truth:** A canonical JSON file (`schemaVersion: 1`) at `~/.config/mcp-sync/config.json` on macOS/Linux, or `%LOCALAPPDATA%\mcp-sync\config.json` on Windows.
- **Targets:** Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, VS Code, Codex, and Kiro. The page does not list Claude Code, Gemini CLI, or any other targets.
- **Preserved settings:** Client-owned fields, comments, target-only servers, and unmanaged remote entries survive a sync. The page says there is no implicit pruning.
- **Backups:** Each changed file keeps one adjacent `.bak` generation with no time-based expiration. Copy backups elsewhere if you need longer history.
- **Dry run:** `sync --dry-run` and `restore --dry-run` show the redacted plan without writing.
- **License:** MIT.
- **Last activity:** The page doesn't show a last-commit date. It lists 184 commits and a security assessment dated 2026-08-09.
- **Stars:** 0 stars, 0 forks, and 0 watchers.

content.content:
**mcpport** (by Abdalkaderdev) is an MIT-licensed CLI for listing, linting, syncing, and converting MCP server configs across Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, and Cursor.

- **Install:** Requires Node 22+. Run with `npx mcpport <command>` or install globally with `npm i -g mcpport`.
- **Commands:** `list`, `lint`, `sync <from> <to>`, and `convert <server> --to <agent>`.
- **Source of truth:** The page doesn't name a central store. The tool reads each agent's own config file, and each agent's format follows that agent's documentation. Claude Code's format serves as the reference shape when translating.
- **User-level configs:** Yes. Targets include `~/.claude.json`, `~/.codex/config.toml`, `~/.gemini/settings.json`, and `~/.cursor/mcp.json`. Claude Code local-scope servers are read-only. Writes only happen with `--apply` (or `--out` for `convert`).
- **Preserves other settings:** Yes. JSON files keep unrelated keys, and `~/.claude.json` keeps key order and non-MCP keys. Codex TOML keeps comments and unrelated tables. CRLF line endings are kept. A JSON file with comments is read but never rewritten.
- **Backups:** Before each write, the target file is copied to `<file>.<timestamp>.bak`, and the new content is written through a temp file and renamed.
- **Dry run:** `sync` is a dry run by default. `convert` prints to stdout unless given `--out` or `--apply`. `list` and `lint` are read-only.
- **License:** MIT.
- **Last activity:** The page doesn't show a last-commit date. It shows 14 commits on `main`.
- **Stars:** 0 stars, 0 forks, and 0 watchers at the time of the page.

content.content:
**Global/user-level MCP config:** No. Ruler only writes project-local MCP files. The docs state: "Ruler never writes MCP configuration files outside your project root." Earlier home-directory targets were removed, so it won't write `~/.claude.json`, `~/.codex/config.toml`, or `~/.gemini/settings.json`.

For Codex, you can point the local config at the project by setting `CODEX_HOME` to the project's `.codex` directory (`export CODEX_HOME="$(pwd)/.codex"`).

`ruler init --global` creates a global Ruler configuration in `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/ruler` (default `~/.config/ruler`), but the docs don't say it applies MCP settings to agents' user-level files.

**Merge vs. overwrite:**
- Set the default globally with `merge_strategy` under `[mcp]` in `ruler.toml`, or per agent under `[agents.<name>.mcp]`. Values are `merge` (default) or `overwrite`.
- The CLI flag `--mcp-overwrite` replaces the native MCP config entirely instead of merging.
- CLI flags take precedence over `ruler.toml`.

The search turned up several open-source tools that sync MCP server configs across Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and Codex. None is clearly the single "canonical" source-of-truth tool you described, and I didn't find brew formulas or confirm npm packages for each.

- **mcp-config-manager** (GitHub, holstein13) manages Claude, Gemini, and Codex config files and can keep them in sync. It has a mode that keeps all three aligned, plus per-client modes. Multi-Client Support - Manages .claude.json, .gemini/settings.json, and Codex configuration files.
- **sync-agents-settings** (GitHub, Leoyang183) treats Claude Code as the source and pushes MCP servers to Gemini CLI and Codex, plus several other agents. It supports a dry-run style diff and doctor check. Configure MCP servers and write instructions once in Claude Code, then sync everywhere with a single command.
- **cc-switch-cli** (GitHub, SaladDay) has an explicit `mcp sync` command with per-app targets. Its docs are the most concrete about the config file locations. Supported apps: claude (default), codex, gemini, opencode, hermes, openclaw, pi. This repo's age is about 221 days.
- **mcp-sync** (EnjoyableWork) is closest to a canonical-config design. It establishes a single local source of truth at ~/.config/mcp-sync/config.json. Its Codex target covers the ChatGPT desktop app, Codex CLI, and IDE extension. A separate PyPI package named mcp-sync is also listed, and it uses a three-tier global, project, and tool config model.
- **vsync** is mentioned in a March 2026 blog post on Codex config management. It reads all configured tool configs and writes the MCP server list to each tool, converting between TOML, JSON, and JSONC.

A useful caveat: a Codex community post notes that MCP servers configured in Codex aren't available to Claude Code. That is the gap these tools fill.

If you need a single canonical tool that covers all three CLIs, mcp-sync (the EnjoyableWork version, with a single source file) and mcp-config-manager are the closest fits from these results. Check each repo's README for current install paths and supported versions before adopting one.

**Install:** A one-line curl installer (`install.sh`) sets up an isolated Python environment, adds an `mcp` command to your PATH, and offers uninstall. Manual install is `git clone` followed by `pip install -e .`, with PyQt6 optional. Python 3.8+ is required.

**Commands:**
- `mcp gui` (or `mcp-gui`), `mcp interactive`, `mcp status`, `mcp uninstall`
- `mcp-config-manager` subcommands: `enable`/`disable` (per server), `enable-all`/`disable-all`, `backup`, `restore`, `add-server`, `delete-server`, `preset` (minimal, webdev, fullstack), `validate`

**Source of truth:** The page doesn't define one. It lists the files it manages: `~/.claude.json`, `~/.gemini/settings.json`, and `~/.codex.json`. Disabled servers are kept in `~/.mcp_disabled_servers.json`. An "All (synced)" mode keeps the configs in sync.

**Codex CLI and Claude Code user configs:** Both are listed as supported. Claude Code is covered via `~/.claude.json`, and Codex via `~/.codex.json`. The page doesn't say how Codex's config format is handled.

**Preserves other settings:** Not explicitly stated. The page says configs are preserved and that the tool uses the same file locations as the original script, but it doesn't describe how unrelated keys are treated when writing.

**Dry-run:** Not mentioned.

**License:** MIT.

**Stars:** 29 stars, 7 forks, 1 open issue, 127 commits. The repo is public.

**Maturity note:** The README says the GUI is "FULLY FUNCTIONAL," but platform testing for Windows and Linux is still listed as in progress.

content.text:
I recommend **cc-switch-cli**, with **sync-agents-settings** as the more cautious alternative. I only researched this and didn't run anything on your machine.

## Main pick: cc-switch-cli

[cc-switch-cli](https://github.com/SaladDay/cc-switch-cli) is free (MIT), runs locally, and supports Claude Code, Codex CLI and Gemini CLI. It keeps one MCP list in its own local database (`~/.cc-switch/cc-switch.db`). For each server you choose which agents get it, and one command writes that into:
- `~/.claude.json`
- `~/.codex/config.toml` (TOML)
- `~/.gemini/settings.json`

It handles the format differences for you. No account is needed: ChatGPT sign-in and WebDAV sync are optional. It's also the most widely used option I found (about 5.4k stars, Homebrew package).

**The catch:** Its README doesn't explicitly say it leaves the rest of those files alone. It does say it writes files safely (temp file, then rename) and has a backup/restore command. The tool also switches API providers, which is a separate feature. If you don't use that feature, it should only touch MCP entries, but check that yourself on the first run (step 3 below).

### Install and first run
1. **Install:** `brew install cc-switch-cli`, or use the `install.sh` script or a release binary from the repo.
2. **Back up the three config files yourself**, since I couldn't confirm it backs them up automatically before an MCP sync:
   `cp ~/.claude.json ~/.claude.json.bak; cp ~/.codex/config.toml ~/.codex/config.toml.bak; cp ~/.gemini/settings.json ~/.gemini/settings.json.bak`
3. **Import, assign and sync:**
   - `cc-switch mcp import --app claude` copies your existing Claude Code servers into the shared list. The docs show `--app claude`; I'm assuming `codex` and `gemini` also work.
   - `cc-switch mcp list` shows the IDs.
   - `cc-switch mcp enable <id> --app codex` and `cc-switch mcp enable <id> --app gemini` choose which agents get each server.
   - `cc-switch mcp sync` writes the files.
   - Run `diff ~/.codex/config.toml.bak ~/.codex/config.toml` (and the same for the other two files). Only the MCP sections should have changed.
4. **From then on:** `cc-switch mcp add` (interactive), then `enable … --app …`, then `cc-switch mcp sync`. You never edit the three files by hand.

## Alternative if keeping your other settings safe matters most: sync-agents-settings

[sync-agents-settings](https://github.com/Leoyang183/sync-agents-settings) treats your Claude Code config as the master list: you add servers with `claude mcp add`, as you do now. It then copies them into Codex and Gemini.

**What it documents that cc-switch-cli doesn't:**
- It keeps unrelated settings.
- It backs up files automatically to `~/.sync-agents-backup/<timestamp>/`.
- It has a `--dry-run` preview.

**Downsides:**
- It's a small project (about 7 stars).
- It doesn't overwrite servers that already exist in Codex or Gemini, so editing a server in Claude won't update the copies.
- It doesn't say whether it removes servers you deleted in Claude.

**Install and run:** `npm i -g sync-agents-settings` (or use `npx sync-agents-settings`), then `sync-agents sync --dry-run`, then `sync-agents sync`.

## Ruled out
- **[Ruler](https://app.unpkg.com/@intellectronica/ruler@0.3.10/files/README.md):** only writes config inside a project folder, never your home-directory configs.
- **[vsync](https://github.com/nicepkg/vsync)** and the Rust **[mcp-sync](https://docs.rs/crate/mcp-sync/latest/source/README.md):** no Gemini CLI support listed.
- **[EnjoyableWork mcp-sync](https://github.com/EnjoyableWork/mcp-sync):** has a good single-list design and promises to keep your other settings, but doesn't list Claude Code or Gemini CLI.
- **[mcpport](https://github.com/Abdalkaderdev/mcpport):** keeps other settings, previews by default and makes backups, but copies from one agent to another (`sync <from> <to>`) instead of keeping one list. It also has no users yet (0 stars).
- **[mcp-config-manager](https://github.com/holstein13/mcp-config-manager):** lists Codex at `~/.codex.json`, not the real `~/.codex/config.toml`.

Whichever you pick, remote servers and environment variables are written differently in each agent (Gemini uses `httpUrl`, for example). After the first sync, open each agent and confirm the servers load.

## Main pick: cc-switch-cli

[cc-switch-cli](https://github.com/SaladDay/cc-switch-cli) is free (MIT), runs locally, and supports Claude Code, Codex CLI and Gemini CLI. It keeps one MCP list in its own local database (`~/.cc-switch/cc-switch.db`). For each server you choose which agents get it, and one command writes that into:
- `~/.claude.json`
- `~/.codex/config.toml` (TOML)
- `~/.gemini/settings.json`

It handles the format differences for you. No account is needed: ChatGPT sign-in and WebDAV sync are optional. It's also the most widely used option I found (about 5.4k stars, Homebrew package).

**The catch:** Its README doesn't explicitly say it leaves the rest of those files alone. It does say it writes files safely (temp file, then rename) and has a backup/restore command. The tool also switches API providers, which is a separate feature. If you don't use that feature, it should only touch MCP entries, but check that yourself on the first run (step 3 below).

### Install and first run
1. **Install:** `brew install cc-switch-cli`, or use the `install.sh` script or a release binary from the repo.
2. **Back up the three config files yourself**, since I couldn't confirm it backs them up automatically before an MCP sync:
   `cp ~/.claude.json ~/.claude.json.bak; cp ~/.codex/config.toml ~/.codex/config.toml.bak; cp ~/.gemini/settings.json ~/.gemini/settings.json.bak`
3. **Import, assign and sync:**
   - `cc-switch mcp import --app claude` copies your existing Claude Code servers into the shared list. The docs show `--app claude`; I'm assuming `codex` and `gemini` also work.
   - `cc-switch mcp list` shows the IDs.
   - `cc-switch mcp enable <id> --app codex` and `cc-switch mcp enable <id> --app gemini` choose which agents get each server.
   - `cc-switch mcp sync` writes the files.
   - Run `diff ~/.codex/config.toml.bak ~/.codex/config.toml` (and the same for the other two files). Only the MCP sections should have changed.
4. **From then on:** `cc-switch mcp add` (interactive), then `enable … --app …`, then `cc-switch mcp sync`. You never edit the three files by hand.

## Alternative if keeping your other settings safe matters most: sync-agents-settings

[sync-agents-settings](https://github.com/Leoyang183/sync-agents-settings) treats your Claude Code config as the master list: you add servers with `claude mcp add`, as you do now. It then copies them into Codex and Gemini.

**What it documents that cc-switch-cli doesn't:**
- It keeps unrelated settings.
- It backs up files automatically to `~/.sync-agents-backup/<timestamp>/`.
- It has a `--dry-run` preview.

**Downsides:**
- It's a small project (about 7 stars).
- It doesn't overwrite servers that already exist in Codex or Gemini, so editing a server in Claude won't update the copies.
- It doesn't say whether it removes servers you deleted in Claude.

**Install and run:** `npm i -g sync-agents-settings` (or use `npx sync-agents-settings`), then `sync-agents sync --dry-run`, then `sync-agents sync`.

## Ruled out
- **[Ruler](https://app.unpkg.com/@intellectronica/ruler@0.3.10/files/README.md):** only writes config inside a project folder, never your home-directory configs.
- **[vsync](https://github.com/nicepkg/vsync)** and the Rust **[mcp-sync](https://docs.rs/crate/mcp-sync/latest/source/README.md):** no Gemini CLI support listed.
- **[EnjoyableWork mcp-sync](https://github.com/EnjoyableWork/mcp-sync):** has a good single-list design and promises to keep your other settings, but doesn't list Claude Code or Gemini CLI.
- **[mcpport](https://github.com/Abdalkaderdev/mcpport):** keeps other settings, previews by default and makes backups, but copies from one agent to another (`sync <from> <to>`) instead of keeping one list. It also has no users yet (0 stars).
- **[mcp-config-manager](https://github.com/holstein13/mcp-config-manager):** lists Codex at `~/.codex.json`, not the real `~/.codex/config.toml`.

Whichever you pick, remote servers and environment variables are written differently in each agent (Gemini uses `httpUrl`, for example). After the first sync, open each agent and confirm the servers load.
